paragraphs.text: 1 The vision of Obadiah. Thus saith the Lord GOD concerning Edom; We have heard a rumour from the LORD, and an ambassador is sent among the heathen, Arise ye, and let us rise up against her in battle. 2 “Behold, I have made thee small among the heathen: thou art greatly despised. 3 The pride of thine heart hath deceived thee, thou that dwellest in the clefts of the rock, whose habitation is high; that saith in his heart, Who shall bring me down to the ground? 4 Though thou exalt thyself as the eagle, and though thou set thy nest among the stars, thence will I bring thee down, saith the LORD. 5 If thieves came to thee, if robbers by night, (how art thou cut off!) would they not have stolen till they had enough? if the grapegatherers came to thee, would they not leave some grapes? 6 How are the things of Esau searched out! how are his hidden things sought up! 7 All the men of thy confederacy have brought thee even to the border: the men that were at peace with thee have deceived thee, and prevailed against thee; they that eat thy bread have laid a wound under thee: there is none understanding in him. 8 Shall I not in that day, saith the LORD, even destroy the wise men out of Edom, and understanding out of the mount of Esau? 9 And thy mighty men, O Teman, shall be dismayed, to the end that every one of the mount of Esau may be cut off by slaughter.

Because Edom dwelt in the rugged mountains, where there are forests and clefts in the rocks, they thought themselves a strong nation that no one could reach and invade. Therefore this book comes as something like the trial of arrogant Edom. In it God appears as a judge, summoning Edom as a breaker of the criminal law. God has sent a messenger to summon the nations to attend the session and to witness the judicial battle in the court, and He brings before them the accused, Edom, who thought that no one could bring him in and try him. Therefore the book begins thus:

“The vision of Obadiah. Thus saith the Lord GOD concerning Edom; We have heard a rumour from the LORD, and an ambassador is sent among the heathen, Arise ye, and let us rise up against her in battle. Behold, I have made thee small among the heathen: thou art greatly despised. The pride of thine heart hath deceived thee, thou that dwellest in the clefts of the rock, whose habitation is high; that saith in his heart, Who shall bring me down to the ground?” [1-3].

The word “vision” in Hebrew is Hazon, and it points to a visible experience. But when it is used as the opening or title of a prophetic book, it often means “observation” or “word.” What Obadiah records here, then, is an observation that he saw or heard by the Spirit of God concerning the trial of Edom by the Lord Himself.

He says, “We have heard a rumour from the LORD,” as though he had received a report from the Lord, that He has sent a messenger among the nations to summon them to attend the trial. So it is said in Jeremiah: “I have heard a rumour from the LORD, and an ambassador is sent unto the heathen, saying, Gather ye together, and come against her, and rise up to the battle” (Jer 49:14). It is a judicial session, but a heated and dangerous one, for He says, “Arise ye, and let us rise up against her in battle.” It is more like a battle than a judicial session, since Edom refuses to appear and thinks that he is above the law.

Since Edom thought that he was above every trial, and reckoned that his dwelling in the mountains among the rock exempted him from coming down to the court, the Lord rebuked him for the pride of his heart, saying to him openly, like one in an interrogation:

“Behold, I have made thee small among the heathen: thou art greatly despised” [2]. You thought, because you dwell on Mount Seir, whose peaks sometimes reach about 2,000 feet above sea level and which is full of rocky clefts, that you were greater than others. Since you exalt yourself in your own eyes, you become very small in My eyes, smaller than the rest of your brothers. For no sin destroys a man’s life like pride, by which he thinks himself a god, yet in the eyes of God he becomes greatly despised, and is exposed to eternal death and destruction. Therefore St. Isaiah the Solitary says: [Watch yourself carefully, avoiding authority, honor, glory and the love of praise as spiritual wounds, and death and destruction as eternal torment]. And the Father Mar Isaac the Syrian says: [Temporal glory is like a rock hidden in the sea, which the sailor does not know until a ship strikes it, and its bottom is torn and it fills with water].

“The pride of thine heart hath deceived thee, thou that dwellest in the clefts of the rock, whose habitation is high; that saith in his heart, Who shall bring me down to the ground?” His heart was lifted up, that is, he exalted himself in his own eyes by his own understanding, since the heart among the Semites meant the center of understanding. By his own understanding, then, his dwelling in the dwellings or caves of the rock, Sela, deceived him. Perhaps by Sela here is meant Mount Seir, high, rugged and full of clefts and caves; or, as some scholars see it, the capital of Edom, “Selah” (Judg 1:36; 2 Kgs 14:7; Isa 16:1); and perhaps it is Petra (rock), which existed in the days of the Nabataeans. In any case, by his human thought, seeing himself hidden among the rocks and settled on the heights, “whose habitation is high,” he thought that no one could bring him down to the ground to enter with him into the court of judgment among the nations.

“Though thou exalt thyself as the eagle, and though thou set thy nest among the stars, thence will I bring thee down, saith the LORD” [4]. Thus God brings down the proud, who seek for themselves the high places of this world. Edom reckoned himself like the eagle, since he set his nest above the mountain peaks among the forests (like an eagle’s nest among the lofty stars). He has become as if among the stars, but this does not mean that he is beyond the reach of God’s hand. Edom carried the mind of the devil, his father, who in his pride exalted himself, as the Lord says to him: “For thou hast said in thine heart, I will ascend into heaven, I will exalt my throne above the stars of God: I will sit also upon the mount of the congregation, in the sides of the north: I will ascend above the heights of the clouds; I will be like the most High. Yet thou shalt be brought down to hell, to the sides of the pit” (Isa 14:13-14). When Satan fell from his humble angelic mind, he desired to set his throne above the stars, and so he was brought down to hell; but the Lord Christ, who is above all creation, came down to us on the earth, and a star came from heaven preaching Him!

“If thieves came to thee, if robbers by night, (how art thou cut off!) would they not have stolen till they had enough? if the grapegatherers came to thee, would they not leave some grapes? How are the things of Esau searched out! how are his hidden things sought up!” [5-6]. Because they dwell in the caves of the rocks, they were also known for the multitude of thieves. The thief enters the hiding places to steal what he needs, that is, whatever is precious. He enters by night while you are asleep, to obtain what they seek. And if grape gatherers come to them, they do not leave the vineyards except with very little of the harvest remaining, which is refuse. This is what thieves and gatherers do; would it then be hard for the Creator to enter the hiding places of Esau (Edom), search their depths, and draw out whatever He wishes for his trial?!

Now, after He has declared to him the folly of his understanding, since his pride destroys him and does not save him, and his heights bring him down and do not uphold him, now He speaks of those on whom he relies: the allies and the wise men.

First, as for his allies, with whom he entered into a covenant, whose bread he ate and with whom he was at peace, the very same will be a witness against him at the trial. Babylon stirred him up to hate his brother and plunder him, and she will be a witness against him after she set a snare under him. The Lord says to him: “All the men of thy confederacy have brought thee even to the border: the men that were at peace with thee have deceived thee, and prevailed against thee; they that eat thy bread have laid a wound under thee: there is none understanding in him” [7]. It is as though He says to him: You were foolish, for you trusted not in the one who saves you but in the one who destroys you... So evil friends do to a man: while they flatter him and share with him feasts and wicked schemes, they turn against him and destroy him.

Second, Edom was known for his wise and understanding men, among them Eliphaz the Temanite (Job 2:11), from Teman, five miles east of Petra in Edom. But God destroys these wise men from Edom: “Shall I not in that day, saith the LORD, even destroy the wise men out of Edom, and understanding out of the mount of Esau? And thy mighty men, O Teman, shall be dismayed, to the end that every one of the mount of Esau may be cut off by slaughter?” [8-9]. Not only did He humble him by withdrawing his friends from the position of defenders to the position of those who set a snare under him and witness against him, but He deprives him even of his wise men who are from Edom, for to him who has, it is given and he has more, and from him who has not, even what he has is taken away.

10 “For thy violence against thy brother Jacob shame shall cover thee, and thou shalt be cut off for ever. 11 In the day that thou stoodest on the other side, in the day that the strangers carried away captive his forces, and foreigners entered into his gates, and cast lots upon Jerusalem, even thou wast as one of them. 12 But thou shouldest not have looked on the day of thy brother in the day that he became a stranger; neither shouldest thou have rejoiced over the children of Judah in the day of their destruction; neither shouldest thou have spoken proudly in the day of distress. 13 Thou shouldest not have entered into the gate of my people in the day of their calamity; yea, thou shouldest not have looked on their affliction in the day of their calamity, nor have laid hands on their substance in the day of their calamity; 14 Neither shouldest thou have stood in the crossway, to cut off those of his that did escape; neither shouldest thou have delivered up those of his that did remain in the day of distress.”

After the Lord had summoned Edom down from his pride and brought him to the court of judgment before the nations, and had declared the futility of his defenders, whether his allies or the wise and understanding men among them, then, before issuing the sentence, He set forth the accusation, announcing the grounds of the verdict...
“For thy violence against thy brother Jacob shame shall cover thee, and thou shalt be cut off for ever” [10].

In his pride he exalted himself against God, reckoning that He would not judge him, and in his wickedness he tyrannized over his brother, who was of his own blood! Truly, whoever does not love God cannot love his brother, and whoever sins against God sins also against his brother. Our relationship with God and with our brothers is interwoven and inseparable; they cannot be isolated from one another. Therefore God reckoned the commandment to love one’s neighbor to be like the love of God and a completion of it.
Wronging others covers a man with shame, and even cuts him off for ever.

He uncovers to him his violence, saying: “In the day that thou stoodest on the other side, in the day that the strangers carried away captive his forces (the foreigners carried off his forces and his wealth into captivity), and foreigners entered into his gates, and cast lots upon Jerusalem, even thou wast as one of them” [11]. He reminds him of the day of the captivity of Jerusalem, when its human and material resources were plundered and carried into captivity, and strangers broke into the city, defiling it and casting lots over its spoils among themselves. So instead of Edom standing as a support for his brother, or even in a position of neutrality, he became like one of those strangers who seized the rights of Jerusalem. It is a hideous picture of one who waits for his brother’s destruction so that he may stretch out his hand and take part in it!

What Edom did he should not have done, for he was bound by seven things, yet he did the opposite. 1. “Thou shouldest not have looked on the day of thy brother in the day that he became a stranger” [21]; you gazed at him like one who desired that day. 2. “Neither shouldest thou have rejoiced over the children of Judah in the day of their destruction”; you were glad at their destruction, though it was fitting for you to grieve over their sufferings, even if they were falling under a just discipline from the Lord. We have seen in Amos that the Lord reproaches those who do not share with those chastened by the Lord in a just chastening, saying: “But they are not grieved for the affliction of Joseph” (Amos 6:6). And in a fatherly discourse on repentance St. Ambrose says: [The first gift is that I know how to grieve deeply with those who sin, for this is the greatest virtue. For it is written: “Neither shouldest thou have rejoiced over the children of Judah in the day of their destruction; neither shouldest thou have looked on their affliction” [12]. O Lord, grant me that the falls of every man may be before me, so that I may bear them with him and not rebuke him in pride, but grieve and weep; for in my weeping for others I weep for myself, saying: “She hath been more righteous than I” (Gen 38:26). 3. “Neither shouldest thou have spoken proudly in the day of distress” [12]. So he turned from desiring to see his brother suffering, to a state of inward joy at his sufferings, and then to uttering words of reproach or of stirring up the enemy against him. In his grief for him, if he could not defend him with a word, he should have kept silent, grieved; but he opens his mouth with evil against him! 4. “Thou shouldest not have entered into the gate of my people in the day of their calamity” [13]. It is a painful assault against God Himself, for he enters the gate of His people. Truly, as the scholar Origen said: [When a man suffers for the sake of the Lord, the Lord Himself is the bearer of the suffering... So every assault on the gate of a suffering man is an assault against the Lord Himself. When our souls are crushed by affliction, the Lord does not stand by merely consoling, but He reckons Himself suffering in us and with us. He upholds us not from outside but by declaring His dwelling within us, that He may bear the cross with us and bring us into the power of His resurrection. 5. “Yea, thou shouldest not have looked on their affliction in the day of their calamity” [13]. Here the look is harsher than it was in the first stage, for in the first it was a look of longing and desire, in gloating, before the sufferings occurred, that is, from afar; but here he sees the sufferings and griefs with his own eyes, and he should have been moved, even if they were his enemies... 6. “Nor have laid hands on their substance in the day of their calamity” [13]; he should have stretched out his hand to support him, but sadly he stretched out his hand to destroy his ability to resist, and so his malice turned from gloating to breaking into his house, to words of evil, and then to action against him. 7. “Neither shouldest thou have stood in the crossway, to cut off those of his that did escape; neither shouldest thou have delivered up those of his that did remain in the day of distress” [14]. This is the most hideous picture, where he stands in the road to seize the fugitives from among them and hand them over as slaves to the enemies! It is an inhuman act!

15 For the day of the LORD is near upon all the heathen: as thou hast done, it shall be done unto thee: thy reward shall return upon thine own head. 16 For as ye have drunk upon my holy mountain, so shall all the heathen drink continually, yea, they shall drink, and they shall swallow down, and they shall be as though they had not been.

Having set forth his many evils in his violence against his brother, He issued the sentence: “For the day of the LORD is near upon all the heathen: as thou hast done, it shall be done unto thee: thy reward shall return upon thine own head. For as ye have drunk upon my holy mountain, so shall all the heathen drink continually, yea, they shall drink, and they shall swallow down, and they shall be as though they had not been” [15-16]. The sentence is passed upon all: “As thou hast done, it shall be done unto thee.” This is the principle or law of the great day of the Lord. As the Lord says: “With what measure ye mete, it shall be measured to you again” (Mt 7:2).

Scholars see that the drinking here is of the cup of the wine of God’s wrath. If God gave His people this cup to drink because of their sins, Edom will drink it more bitterly, and so will all the nations because of their evil, as it is written in the book of Jeremiah: “Take the wine cup of this fury at my hand, and cause all the nations, to whom I send thee, to drink it. And they shall drink, and be moved, and be mad, because of the sword that I will send among them” (Jer 25:15-16)... But here He says: “They shall drink, and they shall swallow down, and they shall be as though they had not been.” That is, whenever they receive a punishment they drink and swallow it, and a more severe punishment appears, so that the former seems as nothing before it.

17 “But upon mount Zion shall be deliverance, and there shall be holiness; and the house of Jacob shall possess their possessions. 18 And the house of Jacob shall be a fire, and the house of Joseph a flame, and the house of Esau for stubble, and they shall kindle in them, and devour them; and there shall not be any remaining of the house of Esau; for the LORD hath spoken it. 19 And they of the south shall possess the mount of Esau; and they of the plain the Philistines: and they shall possess the fields of Ephraim, and the fields of Samaria: and Benjamin shall possess Gilead. 20 And the captivity of this host of the children of Israel shall possess that of the Canaanites, even unto Zarephath; and the captivity of Jerusalem, which is in Sepharad, shall possess the cities of the south. 21 And saviours shall come up on mount Zion to judge the mount of Esau; and the kingdom shall be the LORD’S.”

If this prophecy is addressed to arrogant, unjust Edom, so that he may realize that he receives the recompense of his work, it is also addressed to humbled Zion, to assure her that God does not leave her in her humiliation... He disciplines and shows mercy, allows wounds and binds up.

“But upon mount Zion shall be deliverance, and there shall be holiness; and the house of Jacob shall possess their possessions. And the house of Jacob shall be a fire, and the house of Joseph a flame, and the house of Esau for stubble...” [17-18]. It is a living picture of Zion’s restoration to her strength, her holiness and her dignity. Upon her mountain there shall be deliverance or salvation, for the Cross is raised up to embrace every believing soul, granting it authority to tread on serpents and scorpions. And there shall be holiness, for He makes of it a holy temple in which the Holy Spirit of God dwells; and possessions, for the Lord reigns and possesses the heart as His throne; and He makes it a fire by the fiery Holy Spirit, who burns the house of Esau, that is, the works of the old man, like stubble, and sin cannot stand before it, but is kindled and burned and destroyed, for “there shall not be any remaining of the house of Esau; for the LORD hath spoken it.” So the word of the Lord is fulfilled in us by His fiery Spirit, who leaves no trace of evil within us.

He then speaks of the salvation which is accomplished partly in a literal way by the return of Israel and Judah from captivity, and is fulfilled spiritually in a more perfect way in the New Testament through the Cross.

In this conclusion the children of God inherit the nations that gloated over them at their captivity; they do not merely return to their former condition before the captivity, but inherit the nations along with their return from captivity. It is a spiritual picture of the Church of the New Testament, which has caught in her nets many fish from all nations, tongues and peoples for the sake of her Bridegroom, that He may reign over all.

He says: “And saviours shall come up on mount Zion to judge (to rule) the mount of Esau” [21]. As St. Augustine says: [These saviours are the Apostles who went out from the Jews to preach on the mount of Esau, that is, among the Gentiles, and to catch them for the Kingdom of God... Therefore the book closes with the words: “And the kingdom shall be the LORD’S” [21]. This is the goal of the whole of Holy Scripture, and the goal of what was said in the events of the Lord’s birth: “He shall reign over the house of Jacob for ever; and of his kingdom there shall be no end” (Lk 1:33). And it is said in Revelation: “The kingdoms of this world are become the kingdoms of our Lord, and of his Christ” (Rev 11:15), “Alleluia: for the Lord God omnipotent reigneth” (Rev 16:6).
